extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, narratology students, and creative writers studying narrative voice (e.g., graduate students and advanced undergraduates)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and choosing narrator status and voice (level, person, presence, and functions) for narrative fiction; classifying narrators and understanding their effects (e.g., as in Proust). Useful for literary analysis and for authors deciding narrative posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish grammatical person from narrative posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Common locutions like 'first-person' or 'third-person' are inadequate because they stress a grammatical choice while the novelist's choice is actually between two narrative postures: having the story told by one of its 'characters' or by a narrator outside the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate presence of first-person verbs with autodiegetic narration automatically (examples: Virgil's 'I' vs Crusoe's 'I'). When designing or analyzing narration, first identify whether the narrator belongs to the diegetic universe (is a character) or not, rather than relying solely on grammatical person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterodiegetic vs homodiegetic narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterodiegetic: narrator absent from the story he tells (example: Homer in the Iliad). Homodiegetic: narrator present as a character in the story he tells (example: Gil Blas, Wuthering Heights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify narrators by their relationship to the narrated events; this distinction underpins many narrative effects and should guide choices about perspective, knowledge, and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autodiegetic narrator (narrator is the story's hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong variety of homodiegetic narration in which the narrator is the incontestable hero of his narrative (example: Gil Blas). Genette reserves the term 'autodiegetic' for this unavoidable strong degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use autodiegetic narration when you want the focal consciousness and narrative authority to coincide with the protagonist; be aware this entails constraints on omniscience and scope of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary/bystander homodiegetic narrator (witness-narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A homodiegetic narrator who plays only a secondary role—observer and witness rather than hero (examples: Lockwood, Dr. Watson, Ishmael as varying degrees). There is also a collective witness variant (e.g., the crew of The Nigger of the 'Narcissus').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This posture allows a proximate but limited perspective: the narrator can report and comment without being the central actor, useful for partial knowledge, irony, or framing the hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of narrator presence and pronominal vertigo (anti-patterns and modern use)
rubrics_metrics.description: While absence is absolute, presence admits degrees; shifts in grammatical person (e.g., sudden moves from 'I' to 'he') are conventionally perceived as infractions of an implicit norm and can indicate textual incompleteness or, in modern literature, deliberate experimentation (pronominal vertigo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat abrupt person shifts with care: they can be signs of narrative pathology (accidental/incoherent) or a deliberate modern technique. Examples to consider: Bianchon's sudden shift, Jean Santeuil fluctuations, Borges's 'The Form of the Sword.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Metadiegetic narrative as performative (narrative that 'gives' or 'takes' life)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metadiegetic narrative—especially when uttered in the future tense—can act as a trap that 'takes' (example: the oracle in Oedipus is a metadiegetic narrative that brings about parricide and incest). Narrative has performative power: some narratives 'give life' (Scheherazade), some 'take life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing nested narratives, consider their performative effects: a reported or embedded narrative can function as causal agent within the story's world and drive destiny or action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-axis classification: narrative level × relationship to story
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's status is defined by both its narrative level (extradiegetic vs intradiegetic) and its relationship to the story (heterodiegetic vs homodiegetic), which jointly yield four basic types (examples invoked: Homer, Gil Blas, Scheherazade, Ulysses in IX–XII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the level × relationship grid to classify narrators precisely: it helps map complex narrating systems (multiple narrators, framed tales, metadiegetic layers) and to anticipate constraints on knowledge and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative-choice as aesthetic, not autobiographical proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption of first-person in fiction (Proust's 'I') can be a conscious aesthetic choice and does not necessarily mean the work is an autobiography or a direct expression of the author's life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading or writing, avoid assuming identity between author and narrating 'I'; treat first-person as a narrative posture chosen for discursive needs and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciling autodiegetic 'I' with omniscient commentary (tension of scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: An autodiegetic or first-person narrator may nevertheless be required to present a comprehensive narrative content that overflows the hero's direct knowledge, producing tensions (Proust's Recherche alternates an omnipresent speculative discourse with an autodiegetic stance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you choose a first-person/autodiegetic voice but need wide-ranging or omniscient material, anticipate and plan techniques for integrating outside knowledge (e.g., indirect discourse, stratified narrating instances, authorial commentary) or accept narrative incoherences as an artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merging/blending of hero's and narrator's voices after a revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the narrator's present knowledge and the hero's experienced past converge (e.g., after a final revelation), the hero's 'I thought' can be written as 'I understood'—allowing the hero's imperfect-tense account to coincide with the narrator's present-tense authority; this produces proliferation of indirect discourse and omnitemporality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such merging to create retrospective insight, unify voice, and achieve philosophic or aesthetic closure; but manage shifts carefully to avoid confusing tense/person boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of narrating I and narrated I (Spitzer) — developmental distance
rubrics_metrics.description: In autobiographical-form narratives, the 'narrating I' (erzählendes Ich) and the 'narrated I' (erzähltes Ich) are separated by age/experience, enabling the narrating I to treat the narrated I with irony or condescension; in Proust an additional absolute difference (final revelation/aesthetic vocation) produces a deeper discontinuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing in retrospective first-person, decide the degree of distance and the balance between ironic detachment and identification; distance can permit commentary and moralizing that the younger self could not authoritatively provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator functions — the properly narrative function
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's primary, indispensable role is the properly narrative function: telling the story (the 'story' aspect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All other functions derive from or modulate this primary task; when designing narration, ensure the central narrating function is preserved even as you add metanarrative or ideological layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator functions — directing/metanarrative (stage directions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator can adopt a metalinguistic role to mark articulations, connections, and internal organization of the narrative (stage directions or 'directing indications').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use directing indications to structure long or complex narratives, to signal temporal jumps, or to provide organizing cues to the reader (examples: Cooper, Thomas Mann).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator functions — communication (phatic/conative; orientation to narratee)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator may orient discourse toward a narratee—present, absent, or implied—establishing or maintaining contact (phatic) or acting upon the receiver (conative); such narrators ('raconteurs') may privilege communication over narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistolary forms and Shandean narration exploit this function; choose it when you want an intimate, conversational, or performative relation with the reader/audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator functions — attestation/emotive/testimonial
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator can attest to sources, assert the precision of memories, or report feelings—an emotive/testimonial function linked to the narrator's relation to events and to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use attestation to build trust, register fallibility, or ground subjective recollection (examples: Rousseau's Confessions; moments of present testimony in works like Doctor Faustus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator functions — ideological/didactic (authorized commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator can provide authorized commentary or didactic discourse (the ideological function), explaining or interpreting events, giving speculative judgment or moralization (Balzac and other 'ideological' novelists exemplify this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide who bears the ideological function: an omniscient narrator, an explicit authorial voice, or a character-spokesman. Proust largely reserves ideological commentary to the narrator rather than to characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proustian principle: quasi-monopoly of the ideological function
rubrics_metrics.description: In Proust the ideological/didactic monopoly is quasi-exclusive to the narrator (Marcel); characters are objects of observation, not authorized speakers of speculative discourse, and intellectual conversation is downplayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If emulating a Proustian model, keep speculative or interpretive weight in the narrator's voice; let characters provoke thought rather than voice authoritative doctrines (examples: Bergotte, Vinteuil, Charlus are observed, not spokesmen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative-course suitability: choose form according to discursive needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative course must suit the needs of the discourse: Jean Santeuil's heterodiegetic course proved inadequate for Proust's purposes, leading to conversion to autodiegetic narrating; neither pure objectivity nor pure subjectivity necessarily suffices for complex narrative content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning narrative form, assess whether your chosen narrator can legitimately encompass the material you need (social chronicle, omniscient commentary, interior experience) and be prepared to change posture if the discourse demands it.
